Fake Travel Agent Scam UK: How to Spot and Avoid Holiday Booking Fraud

Fraudsters are impersonating legitimate travel agents and independent travel consultants to steal thousands from UK holidaymakers — here's how to spot the fakes before you book.

By Alex Bacsa · Published 2026-06-27 · 8 min read

fake travel agent scam UKtravel agent fraudholiday booking scamfake travel websitetravel agent verification UK
Key rule: verify through an official route you opened yourself, not the link, number, app, or payment details supplied by the suspicious message.

Being targeted right now? Do this

  1. Stop. Don’t pay, transfer money, or share passwords, PINs, or one-time codes.
  2. Contact your bank on the number on the back of your card if your money or details may be at risk.
  3. Report it — call Action Fraud on 0300 123 2040 (Police Scotland: 101), and forward scam texts to 7726.

What fake travel agent scams look like

Fake travel agent scams work by creating convincing copies of real travel businesses or inventing entirely new ones. Scammers set up websites, social media profiles, and email addresses that closely mimic legitimate travel agents, often using similar names, logos, and branding. They advertise heavily discounted holidays, last-minute deals, or exclusive packages that seem too good to be true. Once you contact them, they build trust through professional-looking communications and pressure you to book quickly before the deal expires.

They then collect your payment (often via bank transfer, gift cards, or cryptocurrency) and personal details including passport information, date of birth, and address. After taking your money, they either disappear entirely, or use your stolen data for identity theft. Some scammers may send fake confirmation emails and itineraries to keep you believing the booking is real until you arrive at the airport and discover nothing has been booked.

Red flags that a travel agent may be fake

  • Pressure to pay immediately or the deal will expire — legitimate travel agents give you time to decide and ask questions.
  • Payment requested only by bank transfer, gift card, or cryptocurrency — real travel agents accept credit cards, debit cards, and established payment methods that offer buyer protection.
  • Website with poor spelling, grammar, or design — professional travel businesses invest in quality websites; typos and clumsy layouts are common in scam sites.
  • No phone number listed, or a number that goes unanswered — genuine travel agents provide multiple contact methods and respond to calls and emails.
  • Prices significantly lower than competitors for the same holiday — if a week in Spain costs £200 when others charge £800, it is almost certainly a scam.
  • No verifiable business registration or ABTA membership — UK travel agents should be registered with ABTA (Association of British Travel Agents) or hold an ATOL licence (Air Travel Organisers' Licensing).
  • Social media account created recently with few followers or engagement — scammers often set up new profiles to avoid detection.
  • Requests for passport details, full address, or bank details before you have paid — legitimate agents ask for these only after booking is confirmed and payment is secure.

How the scam unfolds from first contact to money loss

The scam typically begins when you see an advert on social media, search results, or email offering an attractive holiday deal. You click through to a website that looks professional and similar to real travel agent sites. You browse packages, select a holiday, and are prompted to enter your details and make a payment. The scammer may use urgency tactics — 'only 2 seats left', 'offer ends today' — to rush your decision. You provide your name, email, phone number, passport details, and payment information.

The payment is processed (or appears to be), and you receive a confirmation email that looks authentic, complete with a booking reference and itinerary. You may receive follow-up emails asking for additional information or 'final payments' for extras like travel insurance or airport transfers. Weeks later, when you try to check in online or contact the agent with questions, you discover the website is offline, emails bounce back, or the phone number is disconnected.

You attempt to contact your bank or payment provider, only to learn that the money has already been transferred out of the scammer's account or converted to cryptocurrency. By this point, your personal data — including passport details — is in the hands of criminals and may be used for identity theft or sold to other fraudsters.

How to verify a travel agent is genuine before you book

Start by checking whether the travel agent is registered with ABTA or holds an ATOL licence. Visit the ABTA website and search their member directory by business name — if the agent does not appear, do not book with them. For ATOL protection, check the Civil Aviation Authority's ATOL register online. Next, verify the website domain: type the agent's name into a search engine and compare the URL in the search results with the one you are visiting — scammers often use similar-sounding domain names (e.g., 'travelagents-uk.com' instead of 'travelagents.co.uk').

Call the travel agent using the phone number on their official website (not a number from an email or advert) and ask questions about the holiday — listen for professional responses and local knowledge. Search the agent's name plus 'scam' or 'reviews' on Google and Trustpilot to see if other customers have reported fraud. Ask the agent to send you a formal quote or booking confirmation via email before you pay, and check that the email address matches their official website domain.

If paying by credit card, use this method rather than bank transfer or gift cards, as credit card payments offer chargeback protection. Never pay via cryptocurrency, gift cards, or money transfer services like Western Union — these cannot be reversed if the booking is fake.

What to do immediately if you have already paid a fake travel agent

If you have paid by credit or debit card, contact your bank or card provider immediately — use the number on the back of your card or your online banking app. Report the transaction as fraudulent and request a chargeback. Your bank can often recover the money if you act within 30 days. If you paid by bank transfer, contact your bank straight away and ask them to recall the payment or freeze the recipient's account — this works only if the money has not yet been withdrawn.

If you paid via PayPal, log into your account, find the transaction, and open a dispute or file a claim for an unauthorised payment. If you used a gift card or money transfer service, contact the provider immediately to report the fraud, though recovery is unlikely. Do not send any more money to the scammer, even if they claim there is a problem with your booking or demand a 'correction fee'. Change your passwords for any online accounts you may have used to contact the agent.

If you provided your passport details, contact the UK Passport Service to check if anyone has tried to apply for a replacement passport in your name. Monitor your credit file using a free service like Clearscore or Experian to watch for signs of identity theft.

Reporting fake travel agent fraud in the UK

Report the scam to Action Fraud, the UK's national fraud reporting service, by calling 0300 123 2040 or visiting their website. Provide as much detail as possible: the travel agent's name, website URL, email address, phone number, and the amount you paid. If you received a suspicious email from the fake travel agent, forward it to the NCSC Suspicious Email Reporting Service at report@phishing.gov.uk — this helps the NCSC take down phishing websites. If you were contacted via text message, forward the message to 7726 (a free reporting number).

Report the fake website to the Internet Watch Foundation if it is still online — they work to remove scam sites. If the scammer contacted you via social media, report the profile to the platform (Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, etc.) as a scam. Contact Citizens Advice on 0808 223 1133 if you need support understanding your rights or next steps. Keep copies of all communications with the scammer, screenshots of the website, and your bank statements showing the payment — these will help investigators and support any chargeback claim.

Frequently asked questions

How can I tell if a travel agent website is fake?

Check the domain name carefully — scammers use URLs similar to real agents but with slight differences. Verify the agent is registered with ABTA or holds an ATOL licence by checking the official registers. Look for poor spelling, grammar, or design on the website, and call the phone number listed to hear if it is answered professionally. If prices are significantly cheaper than competitors or the site pressures you to pay immediately, it is almost certainly fake.

I paid a fake travel agent by bank transfer — can I get my money back?

Contact your bank immediately and report the payment as fraudulent. Ask them to recall the transfer or freeze the recipient's account — this only works if the money has not been withdrawn. If the money has already left the account, your bank may still be able to recover it through their fraud team, but this is not guaranteed. Report the scam to Action Fraud on 0300 123 2040 and keep all evidence of the fraud for your bank's investigation.

What should I do if I gave a fake travel agent my passport details?

Contact the UK Passport Service immediately to check if anyone has tried to apply for a replacement passport in your name. Monitor your credit file using a free service like Clearscore or Experian to watch for signs of identity theft. Consider registering with the National Fraud Database to alert lenders that you are a victim of fraud. Report the scam to Action Fraud and provide details of the personal information you shared.

Is it safe to book with a travel agent I found on social media?

Social media is a common platform for fake travel agents. Before booking, verify the agent is registered with ABTA or holds an ATOL licence, check their website domain carefully, and call them using a number from their official website (not from the social media post). Be wary of heavily discounted deals, pressure to pay quickly, and requests to pay by bank transfer or gift card — these are common scam tactics.

What is the difference between a fake travel agent and a legitimate one?

Legitimate travel agents are registered with ABTA or hold an ATOL licence, have professional websites with clear contact details, accept credit card payments, and do not pressure you to pay immediately. They provide formal booking confirmations and are easy to contact if you have questions. Fake agents often have recently created websites, poor design, pressure you to pay by bank transfer or gift card, and disappear after taking your money.
